To capture the temporal progression of symptoms described in clinical notes, we segment each document into time-anchored spans before running our extraction pipeline. The segmentation procedure is informed by the observation that clinical language encodes temporal information through a combination of tense, aspect, and domain-specific temporal expressions (Pustejovsky et al., 2003; Styler et al., 2014). Styler et al. (2014) demonstrate this most concretely for the clinical domain, showing that temporal expressions in discharge summaries follow systematic patterns that differ substantially from newswire. We adapt their annotation schema, originally developed for the THYME corpus, to the psychiatric notes in our dataset by introducing three new temporal categories that capture uncertainty and approximation, both of which are pervasive in mental health documentation.

The relationship between media framing and public opinion formation has occupied scholars across communication studies, political science, and sociology for decades. A central finding is that the way an issue is presented — which aspects are highlighted, which are omitted, and what causal attributions are made — shapes how audiences evaluate both the issue and those associated with it (Entman, 1993; Druckman, 2001; Iyengar, 1991). This effect is not uniform: individual-level factors such as prior attitudes, media literacy, and partisan identity moderate how strongly framing cues are internalized (Zaller, 1992; Levendusky and Malhotra, 2016). Our work situates itself within this tradition while shifting the unit of analysis from the individual reader to the corpus of news articles itself. We operationalize Entman's (1993) four framing functions — problem definition, causal interpretation, moral evaluation, and treatment recommendation — as structured prediction targets, training a sequence-to-sequence model to identify which functions are activated in a given passage and in what configuration. Unlike prior computational work that treats framing as a document-level classification task, this formulation allows us to capture the co-occurrence and ordering of framing functions within a single article.

Faithfulness to source content remains the primary failure mode in abstractive summarization systems, with models frequently generating plausible-sounding but unsupported claims (Maynez et al., 2020; Kryscinski et al., 2020). We build on the entailment-based faithfulness scoring approach of Kryscinski et al. (2020), which frames consistency checking as a natural language inference problem, but replace their fine-tuned BERT backbone with a domain-adapted model and introduce a confidence calibration step to reduce false negatives on long-form documents.

Automated analysis of legal texts has gained traction as court systems accumulate large digitized repositories of case law, statutes, and regulatory filings. Early approaches relied heavily on keyword matching and Boolean retrieval (Turtle, 1995), but the shift toward neural representations has enabled more nuanced modeling of legal reasoning. Zhong et al. (2020) show that legal judgment prediction benefits substantially from explicitly modeling the hierarchical structure of legal documents — charge sheets, fact descriptions, and applicable statutes occupy distinct functional roles, and models that conflate them underperform. Our charge prediction system encodes this hierarchy through a tree-structured attention mechanism, where each level of the document tree receives a separate attention computation whose outputs are then aggregated via a learned weighting.

Language comprehension requires readers to construct mental representations that go beyond the literal content of individual sentences, integrating prior knowledge, discourse context, and pragmatic inference to arrive at a coherent interpretation. A substantial body of psycholinguistic research has established that this process is incremental: readers do not wait until a sentence is complete before generating predictions about upcoming material (Altmann and Kamide, 1999; Levy, 2008; Smith and Levy, 2013). Levy (2008) formalizes this insight as surprisal theory, demonstrating that processing difficulty at each word is proportional to the negative log-probability of that word given prior context under a probabilistic language model. This result has become foundational for both cognitive modeling and NLP evaluation. We extend the surprisal framework to the discourse level, computing surprisal not at the word level but at the level of discourse relations — specifically, testing whether the coherence of an incoming clause, given the rhetorical structure established so far, predicts reading time increments in eye-tracking data.

Gene ontology (GO) term prediction from protein sequence has seen considerable recent progress with the introduction of attention-based architectures that capture long-range dependencies across the amino acid sequence (Kulmanov et al., 2018; Barot et al., 2021). Barot et al. (2021) establish that hierarchical propagation of GO term predictions — enforcing consistency with the ontology's is-a relation during inference — yields measurable improvements in F-max across all three GO subontologies. Our model incorporates a graph neural network layer over the GO DAG that performs this propagation differentiably during training rather than as a post-processing step, allowing the sequence encoder to receive gradient signal from the ontology structure throughout optimization.

Our error analysis reveals a consistent pattern: the model performs well on task-oriented exchanges but struggles when the conversation shifts into socio-emotional territory, such as expressions of frustration or requests for reassurance. This finding is consistent with the broader observation that dialogue systems trained on task completion objectives systematically underweight affective signals (Rashkin et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2018). Rashkin et al. (2019) make this case most compellingly, showing that empathetic responding requires sensitivity to a speaker's emotional state that task-oriented objectives do not incentivize. In our revised training procedure, we incorporate an auxiliary empathy objective derived from their EmpatheticDialogues dataset and evaluation protocol, though we reweight it dynamically based on a classifier that detects emotional salience in the user's turn, rather than applying it uniformly.

Earnings call transcripts have emerged as a rich source of forward-looking language amenable to automated analysis. Linguistic uncertainty in managerial communication has been shown to predict subsequent stock return volatility and analyst forecast dispersion (Jiang et al., 2019; Li, 2010). Building on Li's (2010) dictionary of forward-looking terms and their syntactic context rules, we construct a weakly supervised classifier that generalizes these patterns to multi-sentence spans and handles negation and hedging constructions that the original lexicon treats as edge cases.

The spread of health misinformation across social media platforms is not a uniform process: certain network positions, content features, and posting patterns are consistently associated with higher virality of false claims (Vosoughi et al., 2018; Cinelli et al., 2020). At the content level, emotionally arousing language — particularly language evoking fear or disgust — is a robust predictor of sharing behavior regardless of veracity (Brady et al., 2017; Guo et al., 2019). Brady et al. (2017) quantify this effect on Twitter, demonstrating that each moral-emotional word added to a tweet increases its retweet rate by approximately 20% within politically homogeneous networks. Our misinformation detection system incorporates a moral foundations signal derived from this framework, computed using an expanded version of the Moral Foundations Dictionary that we extend with domain-specific health and risk terminology identified through bootstrapped distributional similarity on a large biomedical corpus.

Event extraction has historically been approached as a pipeline of subtasks — trigger identification, argument detection, and role assignment — each trained independently (Ahn, 2006; Liao and Grishman, 2010). Joint models that address these subtasks simultaneously have been shown to reduce error propagation and improve overall F1 (Yang and Mitchell, 2016; Lin et al., 2020). Lin et al. (2020) demonstrate that cross-sentence context is particularly important for argument role assignment, as argument spans frequently occur outside the sentence containing the trigger. We extend their document-level encoding strategy to a cross-document setting, incorporating coreference chains across documents in the same cluster to resolve arguments that are only fully specified in a preceding or following article.

Lexical features derived from self-referential language have demonstrated predictive validity for depression severity assessments in both clinical interviews and social media posts (Rude et al., 2004; Coppersmith et al., 2014). Coppersmith et al. (2014) provide the most direct evidence in a social media context, linking elevated first-person singular pronoun rates to depression diagnosis in a large Twitter dataset. Our feature set extends their pronoun-based signal with syntactic dependency patterns that capture not just pronoun frequency but the grammatical roles in which self-referential terms appear — subject vs. object position, for instance, having distinct implications for agency and self-construal.

To evaluate our model's sensitivity to pragmatic implicature, we follow the experimental paradigm established in recent behavioral studies of pragmatic reasoning in both humans and language models (Degen, 2015; Jeretic et al., 2020; Ruis et al., 2022). A recurring finding across this literature is that scalar implicature — the inference from 'some' to 'not all' — is context-sensitive and gradient rather than categorical, with informativeness expectations shaped by the broader discourse goal (Degen and Tanenhaus, 2015; Geurts and Pouscoulous, 2009). Degen (2015) formalizes this sensitivity within a Rational Speech Acts (RSA) framework, showing that both contextual and lexical factors modulate implicature strength in a probabilistic speaker model. We adopt the RSA inference procedure as the outer loop of our evaluation metric, replacing the literal listener distribution Degen uses with our neural model's token-level probabilities, allowing direct comparison with human RSA-derived implicature strengths.

Low-resource neural machine translation remains a difficult problem despite substantial progress in high-resource settings. Transfer learning from related high-resource languages has proven effective at bridging this gap, with cross-lingual pre-trained representations enabling reasonable translation quality with minimal parallel data (Zoph et al., 2016; Gu et al., 2018; Conneau et al., 2020). Gu et al. (2018) show that meta-learning across a set of related language pairs produces model initializations that adapt rapidly to new low-resource languages with as few as a few hundred sentence pairs. We build directly on this meta-learning formulation but incorporate a language similarity prior into the task weighting during meta-training, so that typologically closer languages contribute more strongly to the initialization, rather than treating all source tasks uniformly.

The dynamics of norm emergence and enforcement in online communities have attracted growing computational attention. Communities vary substantially in how explicitly their norms are articulated, how consistently they are enforced, and how members signal norm violations to moderators (Chandrasekharan et al., 2018; Fiesler et al., 2018; Matias, 2019). A robust finding is that communities with clearly stated rules exhibit lower rates of norm-violating behavior, though the direction of causality remains contested (Kiesler et al., 2012; Matias, 2019). Chandrasekharan et al. (2018) offer one of the most comprehensive analyses of this dynamic, demonstrating through a large-scale Reddit study that users banned from quarantined communities subsequently reduce their production of hate speech even in other communities — providing evidence that community-level interventions have cross-community behavioral spillovers. Our norm violation detection system is trained on the taxonomy of infraction types Chandrasekharan et al. develop, though we augment it with two additional categories specific to our target platform and re-annotate a subset of their original examples to reconcile labeling inconsistencies we identified.

Automated essay scoring systems have consistently benefited from explicit modeling of discourse coherence, as coherence is a key dimension of writing quality assessments used by human raters (Burstein et al., 2003; Feng et al., 2014; Mim et al., 2019). Mim et al. (2019) show that unsupervised coherence modeling using entity grids outperforms bag-of-words baselines on scoring tasks across multiple prompt types. We adapt their entity grid construction procedure to handle student-generated text, introducing a normalization step for grammatical errors that would otherwise disrupt syntactic parsing and entity tracking.

The lexical composition of sentiment is not simply additive: negation, intensifiers, and contrastive connectives interact in ways that make phrase-level sentiment substantially harder to predict from word-level signals alone (Socher et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2015; Kiritchenko and Mohammad, 2016). Socher et al. (2013) make this case empirically through the Stanford Sentiment Treebank, demonstrating that recursive neural models that compositionally combine sentiment representations across parse tree nodes outperform flat models that treat the sentence as an unstructured bag. Our model adopts this recursive composition principle but operates over dependency trees rather than constituency trees, motivated by the observation that dependency structures are more directly informative about head-modifier sentiment relationships in domain-specific text.

Coreference resolution systems have long grappled with the challenge of resolving pronouns whose antecedents require real-world knowledge inaccessible from the local textual context. The Winograd Schema Challenge formalized this as a benchmark task, and a stream of work has since examined to what extent large language models capture the requisite commonsense reasoning (Sakaguchi et al., 2020; Kocijan et al., 2019; Emami et al., 2019). Kocijan et al. (2019) demonstrate that fine-tuning on a small set of Winograd-style examples using a Winograd-specific training objective substantially improves resolution accuracy on held-out schema instances, suggesting that task-specific signal can partially compensate for gaps in pre-trained knowledge. Our training procedure incorporates a contrastive objective over Winograd pairs, where the model is trained to assign higher probability to the correct antecedent than to the foil by a minimum margin, rather than using the binary cross-entropy formulation of Kocijan et al.

Our results show that legislators' floor speech becomes measurably more partisan in the months preceding competitive elections, a pattern consistent with strategic positioning theory (Mayhew, 1974; Lee, 2009). The magnitude of this effect varies substantially across committees, with legislators on high-visibility committees showing stronger partisan drift. Lee (2009) provides the theoretical framework for understanding this variation: partisan conflict serves expressive and organizational functions for the party that are distinct from — and sometimes in tension with — the goal of passing legislation. Our computational operationalization of 'partisan expressivity' draws on this distinction, separately modeling issue position-taking and rhetorical intensity as two components of the broader construct, rather than collapsing them into a single dimension as most prior quantitative work has done.

Text mining of biomedical literature for protein-protein interaction (PPI) extraction has been an active area since the early 2000s, with progress tracked through a series of shared tasks (Krallinger et al., 2008; Pyysalo et al., 2008). The most persistent challenge is generalizing across corpora annotated under different relation schemas. Pyysalo et al. (2008) demonstrate that cross-corpus training improves recall at an acceptable precision cost when the schemas are first harmonized through a mapping layer. We extend their harmonization approach to a multi-corpora setting with five source schemas, using a learned schema embedding to perform soft alignment rather than the hard mapping rules they define manually.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems have shown that grounding generation in retrieved passages substantially reduces hallucination rates in open-domain question answering (Lewis et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2023; Guu et al., 2020). A key limitation of the standard RAG setup is that retrieval is performed once at query time, with the retrieved context held fixed throughout generation. Lewis et al. (2020) identify this as a bottleneck for multi-hop questions, where intermediate reasoning steps would benefit from targeted re-retrieval. Our system implements iterative retrieval interleaved with generation, using the partially generated answer as an updated query at each step, building on the single-pass retrieval architecture of Lewis et al. but restructuring the generation loop to allow dynamic context updates.

Gender stereotyping in language has been documented across multiple modalities, from word embeddings (Bolukbasi et al., 2016; Caliskan et al., 2017) to co-reference systems (Rudinger et al., 2018; Zhao et al., 2018) to downstream applications such as resume screening and machine translation (Prates et al., 2020; Stanovsky et al., 2019). A foundational insight is that these biases are not arbitrary: they reflect and reproduce social stereotypes present in training corpora, with occupational and role-based associations being among the most persistent (Bolukbasi et al., 2016; Garg et al., 2018). Garg et al. (2018) trace the diachronic evolution of these associations across decades of text, showing that word embedding spaces reliably recapitulate historical shifts in gender-occupational norms documented by sociologists. Our debiasing method takes their historical embedding trajectories as a signal for which dimensions of the embedding space carry the strongest stereotypic associations, using them to define the gender subspace that our projection-based intervention targets — rather than relying on a small set of seed word pairs as prior geometric debiasing methods do.

Graph-based dependency parsing with maximum spanning tree decoding has been shown to produce higher accuracy on long-distance dependencies than transition-based alternatives, at the cost of higher computational complexity (McDonald et al., 2005; Koo and Collins, 2010). McDonald et al. (2005) demonstrate that factoring the scoring function over individual arcs — while ignoring higher-order interactions — already yields competitive performance and tractable inference. Our parser retains this arc-factored scoring structure but replaces the linear scoring model with a biaffine attention mechanism over contextualized token representations, allowing richer feature interactions without sacrificing the MST decoding guarantee.

Social media has emerged as a surveillance resource for tracking the spread and public perception of infectious disease outbreaks. Platforms like Twitter have been used to monitor influenza incidence, vaccine hesitancy, and public compliance with non-pharmaceutical interventions, often yielding signals days ahead of official reporting systems (Lampos and Cristianini, 2010; Paul and Dredze, 2011; Odlum and Yoon, 2015). Lampos and Cristianini (2010) establish a regression framework linking keyword frequency time series to flu incidence rates reported by health agencies, demonstrating meaningful correlation even with a simple bag-of-words representation. We adapt this regression framework to a multi-pathogen setting, replacing the fixed keyword set with a dynamically updated lexicon and incorporating geographic stratification to account for regional variation in both platform usage and disease prevalence.

Cross-domain generalization in named entity recognition has been a persistent challenge, with models trained on newswire data consistently degrading when applied to clinical, legal, or social media text (Daume III, 2007; Blitzer et al., 2006; Jiang and Zhai, 2007). Domain adaptation approaches have sought to address this through a variety of mechanisms: feature augmentation (Daume III, 2007), instance weighting (Jiang and Zhai, 2007), and more recently, adversarial training to encourage domain-invariant representations (Li et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2019). Daume III (2007) proposes a particularly elegant solution — augmenting each feature with domain-specific and domain-general copies — showing that this simple transformation is equivalent to a more complex kernel-based approach and yields strong empirical results across several NLP tasks. Our adaptation procedure applies this augmentation principle at the representation level rather than the feature level, creating domain-specific and shared transformer heads whose outputs are interpolated based on a learned domain confidence score estimated from the input text.

Framing hate speech detection purely as binary classification has been criticized for obscuring the heterogeneous nature of harmful content and producing models that generalize poorly across platforms and communities (Fortuna and Nunes, 2018; Davidson et al., 2017; Waseem and Hovy, 2016). Davidson et al. (2017) provide a compelling illustration of this fragility, showing that a classifier trained on one Twitter dataset achieves near-chance performance on a second dataset collected under a different keyword strategy, despite high within-dataset accuracy. Their fine-grained taxonomy — distinguishing hate speech, offensive language, and neither — forms the organizational backbone of our annotation scheme, though we disaggregate 'offensive language' into subcategories that reflect the different harm mechanisms identified in our qualitative analysis of the target platform.

Automatic evaluation of long-form text generation remains contested, with reference-based metrics such as ROUGE and BLEU correlating poorly with human judgments in open-ended settings (Novikova et al., 2017; Reiter, 2018; Gehrmann et al., 2021). Reiter (2018) presents a structured analysis of why automatic metrics fail for NLG evaluation, identifying content selection, fluency, and adequacy as orthogonal dimensions that aggregate metrics conflate. Our evaluation protocol separates these dimensions, assessing each with a dedicated automatic proxy where available and falling back to human judgment where not — a decomposition we derive from Reiter's framework but instantiate using more recent learned metrics for the fluency and adequacy components.

The concept of social capital — broadly, the resources accessible through social network ties — has been operationalized in computational work through a range of network-structural proxies, from degree centrality to bridging coefficients (Burt, 2004; Putnam, 2000; Lin, 2001). Burt (2004) demonstrates empirically that individuals who bridge structural holes — gaps between otherwise disconnected network clusters — generate information advantages that translate into measurable career and innovation outcomes. Our network construction procedure builds on Burt's structural hole formalism, computing constraint scores for each node as in his original specification but aggregating them at the community level to produce a community-level bridging score, which we then use as a predictor in our regression models.

For morphologically rich languages with limited annotated resources, data augmentation through morphological inflection has proven a reliable strategy for improving downstream task performance (Anastasopoulos and Neubig, 2019; Bergmanis and Goldwater, 2018; Nicolai et al., 2020). The core insight is that inflectional paradigms encode systematic form-meaning relationships that, if exploited, can multiply labeled examples at low cost. Anastasopoulos and Neubig (2019) demonstrate this most cleanly in a cross-lingual transfer setting, showing that inflecting training data into underrepresented morphological forms before transfer leads to consistent POS tagging improvements across a diverse language sample. We build on their augmentation pipeline but replace the rule-based inflector with a neural inflection model trained on UniMorph paradigm tables, allowing the augmentation to handle irregular paradigms that the original rule system cannot.

Post-hoc analysis of our model's errors reveals a systematic tendency to underestimate risk in cases involving indirect expressions of suicidal ideation — allusions, metaphors, and hypotheticals rather than explicit statements. This mirrors findings from clinical research showing that high-risk individuals often communicate distress obliquely, particularly in text-based communication where stigma concerns are heightened (Joiner, 2005; Klonsky et al., 2016; Gould et al., 2012). Joiner (2005) formalizes the behavioral signals that precede suicidal crises within the Interpersonal Theory of Suicide, identifying thwarted belongingness and perceived burdensomeness as the key psychological drivers. Our lexical features are augmented with proxies for these constructs derived from Joiner's theoretical dimensions, operationalized through a combination of seed lexicons and distributional expansion on a mental health forum corpus.

Argument structure has been modeled at multiple granularities, from claim-premise pairs (Palau and Moens, 2009; Habernal and Gurevych, 2017) to full argument graphs capturing attack and support relations (Stab and Gurevych, 2017; Lawrence and Reed, 2019). Stab and Gurevych (2017) establish that student essays exhibit predictable argumentative structure, with claims, premises, and major claims occupying characteristic positions in the document, a finding that has driven subsequent work on structure-aware classifiers. We extend their annotation scheme to persuasive social media posts, where argumentative structure is less formulaic and often compressed into single sentences combining claim and evidence within a single span.

The question of whether grammatical complexity is distributed uniformly across the world's languages or varies systematically with social and demographic factors has attracted considerable attention in recent years (Trudgill, 2011; Lupyan and Dale, 2010; Dahl, 2004). Population size, degree of language contact, and proportion of adult second-language learners have all been proposed as predictors of morphological simplification, though the evidence remains mixed (Bentz and Winter, 2013; Sinnemäki and Di Garbo, 2018). Lupyan and Dale (2010) offer one of the most influential quantitative investigations, demonstrating across a sample of nearly 2,000 languages that morphological complexity correlates negatively with population size and degree of exogamy — larger, more externally connected speech communities tend toward simpler morphological systems. Our predictive model of morphological complexity uses Lupyan and Dale's predictor variables as features, but replaces their cross-sectional regression design with a Bayesian hierarchical model that accounts for genealogical relatedness among languages in the sample.

A key challenge in summarizing scientific articles is identifying which information constitutes a contribution versus background, motivation, or methodology. Section-based heuristics have long been used as a proxy, but these break down for papers that do not follow conventional structures (Teufel and Moens, 2002; Cohan et al., 2018). Cohan et al. (2018) show that discourse structure — specifically, the section-level rhetorical roles of passages — is a strong predictor of summarization-relevance in long scientific documents, outperforming purely content-based signals. We incorporate a discourse role classifier into our summarization pipeline, trained on Cohan et al.'s discourse labels but applied to a different label granularity: rather than section-level roles, we predict sentence-level rhetorical functions, necessitating re-annotation of a subset of the original corpus at finer resolution.

Distant supervision for relation extraction assumes that any sentence containing two entities known to stand in a given relation expresses that relation — an assumption that introduces substantial label noise (Mintz et al., 2009; Riedel et al., 2010). Riedel et al. (2010) relax this assumption by modeling relation expression as at-least-one among all sentences mentioning an entity pair, yielding cleaner training signal. Our multi-instance learning setup follows Riedel et al.'s at-least-one formulation but extends it to the multi-label case, where an entity pair may simultaneously participate in several distinct relation types.

Cognitive load theory holds that working memory has a limited capacity and that instructional design should minimize extraneous processing demands to maximize the resources available for learning (Sweller, 1988; Paas et al., 2003; van Merriënboer and Sweller, 2005). Sweller (1988) introduced the distinction between intrinsic load, determined by the complexity of the material itself, and extraneous load, introduced by poor instructional design — a distinction that has shaped decades of subsequent research and pedagogical practice. Our text complexity scoring system operationalizes the intrinsic/extraneous distinction computationally, treating content-driven syntactic complexity as a proxy for intrinsic load and formatting and presentation features as proxies for extraneous load, and combining them via a model trained on comprehension outcome data.

Reasoning about physical and causal properties of everyday situations has emerged as a critical capability for language models deployed in grounded settings. Benchmarks such as PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), HellaSwag (Zellers et al., 2019), and PhysicalIQA have probed this capacity with varied results, finding that even large models show systematic gaps when surface heuristics are removed (Gururangan et al., 2018; Niven and Kao, 2019). Zellers et al. (2019) construct HellaSwag using adversarial filtering — iteratively retraining a discriminator and removing examples it can solve using shallow cues — yielding a dataset on which machines lag substantially behind humans despite high performance on the unfiltered version. Our dataset construction pipeline adopts this adversarial filtering strategy but applies it at the feature level rather than the model level, identifying and removing examples solvable by a suite of hand-crafted surface features before involving neural discriminators, so that the filtering proceeds in interpretable stages.

Legal reasoning about precedent requires identifying not only whether a prior case is factually similar to the current one, but also whether the rule articulated in the prior case applies given the material differences between the two situations. This is sometimes called case-based reasoning (CBR), and its computational modeling has a long history in AI and law (Ashley, 1990; Brüninghaus and Ashley, 2003; Zhong et al., 2020). Ashley (1990) formalized the role of dimensions — legally relevant features along which cases can differ — in structuring the comparison between current cases and precedents, showing that dimension-based representations support more principled analogical reasoning than flat feature vectors. Our neural case retrieval system incorporates a structured dimension layer that encodes these legally salient contrasts, learned from annotated case pairs rather than hand-crafted as in Ashley's original HYPO system.

The capacity of multilingual models to transfer across languages zero-shot has been a central area of investigation since the release of mBERT and XLM (Devlin et al., 2019; Conneau and Lample, 2019; Pires et al., 2019). Transfer quality varies substantially across language pairs and tasks, with typological distance, script overlap, and training data size all implicated as contributing factors (Lauscher et al., 2020; Hu et al., 2020). Pires et al. (2019) provide one of the first systematic analyses of mBERT's zero-shot transfer, finding that shared wordpiece vocabulary is a necessary but insufficient condition for successful transfer, and that structural similarity between languages matters independently. We use their typological distance measures as a covariate in our meta-regression over cross-lingual transfer results, but recompute the distances using more recently published typological databases that cover a larger and more genealogically diverse language sample than was available to Pires et al.

Our model's performance degrades noticeably on targets that were absent from the training distribution — a generalization failure consistent with findings on cross-target stance transfer (Augenstein et al., 2016; Allaway and McKeown, 2020). Allaway and McKeown (2020) demonstrate that shared topical framing across targets can be leveraged to improve zero-shot stance generalization through topic-grouped training. We incorporate their topic-grouping signal into our training curriculum, reordering batches by topic cluster rather than randomly, though we derive the topic clusters from our own corpus using LDA rather than the predefined groupings in their dataset.

Constituency parsing in morphologically rich languages is complicated by the high degree of ambiguity introduced by free word order and rich inflectional paradigms. Tsarfaty et al. (2010) demonstrate that joint morphological disambiguation and syntactic parsing yields substantially better results than pipelined approaches for Hebrew, establishing that the two tasks are deeply interdependent in such languages. Our system extends this joint modeling principle to a multilingual setting, replacing the language-specific morphological analyzer used by Tsarfaty et al. with a universal morphological tagger trained on Universal Dependencies data, allowing the joint model to generalize across language families without hand-crafted morphological resources.

A growing body of research has examined the ways in which algorithmic recommendations on social media platforms shape political information consumption. Filter bubbles — environments in which algorithmic curation selectively exposes users to content consistent with their prior beliefs — have been proposed as a key mechanism of political polarization (Pariser, 2011; Sunstein, 2017; Flaxman et al., 2016). Flaxman et al. (2016) provide one of the most rigorous empirical tests of this hypothesis using web browsing data, finding that while social media does increase ideological segregation in news consumption, direct navigation to news sites is associated with even stronger segregation than algorithmic exposure. Our analysis replicates their regression design on a more recent dataset spanning the 2020 U.S. election cycle, adding a platform stratification layer that distinguishes among recommendation mechanisms across four major social platforms rather than treating social media as a monolithic source.

Recent advances in pre-trained language models have been accompanied by growing concern about their tendency to encode and amplify social biases present in training corpora. Probing classifiers have emerged as a standard diagnostic tool for identifying what information is encoded in contextual representations (Conneau et al., 2018; Hewitt and Liang, 2019; Tenney et al., 2019). Hewitt and Liang (2019) introduce a selectivity criterion for probing — comparing probe accuracy against a control probe with a heavily constrained hypothesis class — arguing that probes which outperform their controls by a large margin are likely recovering genuine linguistic structure rather than exploiting incidental statistical regularities. We adopt their selectivity criterion as our primary diagnostic for bias probes, extending it to a multi-attribute setting where probes target intersectional identity combinations rather than single demographic axes.

The identification of opinion holders in news text — sometimes called source attribution — is an important subtask for opinion mining systems that need to distinguish between a journalist's own framing and the positions being reported on behalf of others. Wiebe et al. (2005) introduce a richly annotated corpus for subjective language that includes source attribution as a central annotation layer, demonstrating through inter-annotator agreement analysis that subjective language can be reliably identified and that source information is recoverable from surface linguistic cues in the majority of cases. Our opinion source extraction system draws on the cue taxonomy developed by Wiebe et al. — distinguishing direct, indirect, and implicit attribution patterns — but applies it to parliamentary debate transcripts, where attribution conventions differ substantially from newswire and require several additional cue categories specific to legislative discourse.

Automatic evaluation of dialogue coherence has relied heavily on next-utterance retrieval tasks, in which a model must select the correct response from a pool of candidates. Lowe et al. (2015) introduce the Ubuntu Corpus benchmark under this paradigm and establish strong baselines, showing that dual-encoder architectures trained on large conversational datasets can capture substantial coherence information. Subsequent work has identified serious limitations of this evaluation paradigm, however, noting that retrieval accuracy correlates poorly with human judgments of response quality in open-domain settings (Liu et al., 2016; Novikova et al., 2017). We retain the dual-encoder architecture introduced by Lowe et al. as the backbone of our coherence scorer, but replace the retrieval objective with a contrastive ranking loss over human-annotated coherence judgments, directly addressing the correlation problem identified in subsequent critique.

Cross-lingual word embeddings have made it possible to transfer NLP models to languages with limited labeled data by mapping monolingual embedding spaces into a shared multilingual space. Artetxe et al. (2018) show that this mapping can be learned with minimal supervision — as few as 25 seed word pairs — by exploiting the structural similarity of independently trained monolingual spaces through iterative Procrustes alignment. The robustness of their self-learning procedure to initialization noise is a key finding, as prior work had assumed dense bilingual dictionaries were necessary. Our cross-lingual transfer system for low-resource dependency parsing uses Artetxe et al.'s alignment procedure as a preprocessing step, but applies it over subword embedding spaces rather than word-level embeddings, which we find substantially reduces the vocabulary mismatch problem for morphologically rich target languages.

The computational study of narrative has drawn on a range of theoretical traditions, from Proppian morphology to schema theory to more recent work on event schemas and script knowledge (Schank and Abelson, 1977; Chambers and Jurafsky, 2008; Mostafazadeh et al., 2016). Chambers and Jurafsky (2008) demonstrate that narrative event chains — sequences of events sharing a protagonist, extracted from large corpora via coreference chains — can be learned in an unsupervised fashion and used to predict missing events with above-chance accuracy. This work establishes that distributional statistics over event co-occurrence encode meaningful narrative structure. Our story understanding model builds on the narrative chain representation of Chambers and Jurafsky, replacing their verb-argument co-occurrence statistics with contextualized event representations derived from a pretrained language model, and extending the chain structure to a graph that captures non-sequential causal and temporal relations.

Automatic detection of scientific claims in biomedical literature has received growing attention in the context of evidence synthesis and systematic review automation. Achakulvisut et al. (2019) demonstrate that claim detection framed as a sentence classification problem achieves reasonable performance on abstracts from randomized controlled trials, with the key finding that intervention, outcome, and population spans are strong predictors of claim-bearing sentences. Our pipeline targets full-text articles rather than abstracts and reformulates claim detection as a span extraction task rather than sentence classification, motivated by Achakulvisut et al.'s finding that relevant information is unevenly distributed within sentences — a granularity problem that sentence-level labels cannot capture.

Grounding in human-robot interaction research refers to the process by which interlocutors establish and maintain mutual understanding of the content and intent of communicative acts (Clark and Brennan, 1991). Failure to achieve grounding is a leading cause of task breakdown in human-robot collaborative settings, particularly when the robot's understanding of an instruction diverges from the human's intent without either party detecting the mismatch. Clark and Brennan (1991) formalize grounding as a collaborative process involving presentation and acceptance moves, a framework that has informed both theoretical and computational treatments of dialogue. We operationalize their grounding criterion — that mutual belief in uptake must be established for a contribution to be grounded — as a trainable classifier over dialogue state representations, using it to detect likely grounding failures before they propagate into subsequent turns.

The social model of disability holds that the barriers faced by disabled individuals are primarily social and structural in origin rather than intrinsic to impairment (Oliver, 1990; Shakespeare, 2006). This framing has important implications for how disability is represented and discussed in public discourse, and by extension for how NLP systems trained on such discourse may encode or perpetuate ableist assumptions. Oliver (1990) provides the foundational articulation of this model, distinguishing impairment — the physical or cognitive characteristic — from disability — the social disadvantage produced by environments designed without accommodation for that characteristic. Our analysis of disability representation in large language models uses this distinction as an organizing principle, separately examining how models represent impairment language versus social participation and barrier language.

Semantic textual similarity — the task of assessing the degree to which two sentences convey the same meaning — has been a central benchmark for sentence representation models since the introduction of the STS tasks at SemEval (Agirre et al., 2013). Agirre et al. (2013) establish the regression-to-human-judgment paradigm that has dominated the field, showing that Pearson correlation with crowdsourced similarity ratings is a stable and reproducible evaluation criterion across domains. Several concerns about this paradigm have since been raised: the ratings conflate semantic equivalence with topical similarity, and the crowdsourcing methodology introduces annotator disagreement that aggregate correlation scores obscure. We retain Pearson correlation as a secondary metric for comparability with prior work but introduce a primary evaluation protocol derived from Agirre et al.'s annotation process, disaggregating the ratings by domain and annotator background to surface the sources of variance their aggregate scores suppress.

Conversational question answering — in which questions are posed sequentially with reference to a shared context and each question may depend on previous turns — presents challenges not present in single-turn QA (Reddy et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2018). Coreference and ellipsis across turns mean that many questions are not interpretable without the conversation history, and models must implicitly resolve these dependencies to produce correct answers. Choi et al. (2018) demonstrate through the QuAC dataset that conversational history is essential for performance, with ablations showing large accuracy drops when prior turns are removed. Our model incorporates a history encoding mechanism derived from Choi et al.'s turn-stacking approach but applies a learned attention over history turns rather than concatenating them uniformly, allowing the model to selectively weight earlier context based on the current question.

The relationship between linguistic complexity and reading difficulty has long been studied in readability research, with early formulas relying on surface proxies such as word length and sentence length (Flesch, 1948; Gunning, 1952). More recent work has demonstrated that syntactic complexity — measured through parse tree depth, dependency length, or the frequency of subordinate clauses — is a stronger predictor of comprehension difficulty than surface features alone (Schwarm and Ostendorf, 2005; Vajjala and Meurers, 2012). Schwarm and Ostendorf (2005) show that combining syntactic and surface features in an SVM classifier substantially outperforms either feature class in isolation, a finding that motivated a generation of feature-engineering approaches to readability. Our readability model starts from Schwarm and Ostendorf's feature taxonomy but learns representations of syntactic complexity directly from parse trees using a graph neural network, replacing their hand-crafted syntactic features with learned ones while preserving the combination with surface features.

A persistent finding in computational humor research is that incongruity — the violation of an established expectation — is a necessary if not sufficient condition for humor (Mihalcea and Strapparava, 2005; Yang et al., 2015; Hempelmann and Ruch, 2005). Mihalcea and Strapparava (2005) operationalize this computationally through a dataset of one-liners paired with non-humorous rewritten versions, demonstrating that a combination of semantic relatedness and semantic distance features can distinguish the two with above-baseline accuracy. The pairing methodology they introduce — constructing minimal pairs that differ only in the presence or absence of the incongruous element — has since become a standard data collection strategy. Our dataset construction follows this minimal pair design but uses crowdworkers to generate the non-humorous variants under structured guidelines, rather than relying on the author-generated variants of Mihalcea and Strapparava, which subsequent analysis has shown to differ along multiple dimensions simultaneously.

Temporal relation extraction — identifying whether one event precedes, follows, or is simultaneous with another — is a prerequisite for downstream tasks requiring timeline reconstruction from text. The TimeML annotation scheme (Pustejovsky et al., 2003) established a widely adopted framework for representing temporal information, distinguishing events, temporal expressions, and the relations among them. Chambers et al. (2014) demonstrate that global constraints over event graphs — enforcing transitivity of temporal relations — substantially reduce inconsistencies in extracted relation sets compared to local pairwise classification. Our relation extraction system uses Chambers et al.'s transitivity constraint as a post-inference consistency enforcement step, but applies it through integer linear programming over a richer relation vocabulary that includes aspectual and causal relations not covered in their original formulation.

The use of crowdsourcing for linguistic annotation has raised persistent questions about the reliability and validity of judgments from non-expert workers relative to trained annotators. Snow et al. (2008) conduct an influential comparative study demonstrating that aggregated crowdsourced judgments match expert annotations on a range of NLP tasks — including word sense disambiguation, textual entailment, and temporal ordering — when a sufficient number of workers are used per item. This result has been widely cited as justification for crowdsourced annotation pipelines, though subsequent work has identified important boundary conditions around task complexity and worker selection. We design our annotation pipeline following Snow et al.'s aggregation approach, using majority vote with a quality filter based on worker agreement, but extend their quality control framework with an adaptive routing mechanism that identifies difficult items in real time and routes them to a smaller pool of verified high-quality workers.

Character-level models for text classification have been shown to capture morphological and orthographic regularities that word-level models miss, particularly for noisy social media text and morphologically rich languages (Zhang et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2016). Zhang et al. (2015) demonstrate that deep character-level convolutional networks can match or exceed word-level baselines on a range of text classification tasks, without any explicit tokenization or linguistic preprocessing. Their result is particularly striking on tasks involving user-generated content, where spelling variation and non-standard forms pose challenges for vocabulary-based approaches. We adapt Zhang et al.'s convolutional architecture to a byte-level input representation, replacing the character alphabet with raw UTF-8 bytes to handle multilingual and code-switched input without language-specific preprocessing, and add a residual connection structure that improves gradient flow for the deeper configurations their ablations identified as most effective.

Protest event analysis from news media has relied predominantly on hand-coded event catalogs, which are expensive to produce and difficult to scale. Automated approaches using structured event extraction pipelines have been developed to address this, but they tend to require manually crafted extraction patterns that do not generalize across news sources or languages (Hanna et al., 2017; Lorenz et al., 2021). Hanna et al. (2017) show that even noisy automated extraction yields data of sufficient quality for aggregate analyses of protest trends when systematic error patterns are characterized and corrected for. Their error characterization methodology — comparing automated extractions against a gold standard on a stratified random sample — informs our validation procedure, which we apply across multiple languages simultaneously and extend with a cross-source consistency check not present in their original design.

Predicting the persuasiveness of arguments has applications in automated debate coaching, argument generation, and misinformation detection. Habernal and Gurevych (2016) demonstrate that pairwise argument quality judgments — asking annotators which of two arguments is more convincing rather than rating each in isolation — produce more reliable annotations than absolute quality ratings, a finding consistent with psychophysical research on comparative judgment. Their UKPConvArg dataset, collected under this pairwise paradigm, has become a standard benchmark. We adopt the pairwise annotation methodology of Habernal and Gurevych for our dataset collection but extend the comparison to argument pairs drawn from different claim contexts, testing whether perceived persuasiveness is claim-specific or reflects more general stylistic properties of argumentation.

The relationship between syntactic structure and translation difficulty has been examined from multiple angles, with constituent reordering identified as a key source of both human translator difficulty and machine translation error (Gildea and Jurafsky, 2002; Fox, 2002; Birch et al., 2008). Birch et al. (2008) quantify this reordering difficulty through a metric based on Kendall's tau over word-level alignments, demonstrating that the metric correlates with human adequacy assessments across language pairs at varying typological distances. Our evaluation framework adopts their reordering metric as one component of a multi-dimensional translation difficulty score, but applies it at the phrase level rather than the word level, which we show better captures the difficulty introduced by long-distance constituent movement in verb-final languages.

The study of linguistic accommodation — the phenomenon by which interlocutors adjust their language to match their conversation partners — has been substantially advanced by the availability of large conversational corpora. Danescu-Niculescu-Mizil et al. (2011) demonstrate through an analysis of movie dialogue and Twitter conversations that accommodation is pervasive and asymmetric: lower-status interlocutors accommodate more strongly to higher-status ones, with function word matching being a particularly robust signal. This asymmetry provides a linguistic index of social power that does not depend on explicit status markers. Our analysis of power dynamics in organizational email corpora builds on Danescu-Niculescu-Mizil et al.'s function word matching methodology, extending it to a longitudinal setting in which accommodation patterns are tracked over individual employees' tenure to detect status transitions that are not reflected in official organizational records.

Distant supervision for biomedical relation extraction assumes that co-occurring entities known to participate in a target relation in a curated database are likely to express that relation in the surrounding text (Mintz et al., 2009; Percha and Altman, 2018). Percha and Altman (2018) apply this approach at scale to drug-gene interaction extraction, using DrugBank as a supervision source and demonstrating that the resulting extractions substantially expand the known drug-gene interaction network when combined with careful deduplication. A key contribution is their dependency path clustering method for grouping syntactically similar extraction patterns, which reduces noise from spurious co-occurrences. We adopt their dependency path clustering approach for our protein-protein interaction extraction system, generalizing the clustering procedure from binary dependency paths to subgraph patterns that capture interactions involving more than two participants.

Language grounding — the mapping between linguistic expressions and perceptual or situational referents — has been studied in both cognitive science and robotics, with particular attention to reference resolution in situated dialogue. Kazemzadeh et al. (2014) introduce the ReferItGame dataset, demonstrating through human-human data collection that referring expression comprehension can be operationalized as image-region retrieval and that humans reliably produce and interpret such expressions using a combination of object properties, spatial relations, and discourse context. Their data collection paradigm — pairing human players who must identify the same image region through natural language without seeing each other's screens — has since become standard in vision-language research. We build on this paradigm for our dataset of referring expressions in medical images, adapting the game setup to a radiology reading context in which players describe lesion locations using anatomical and relational language unavailable in the original general-domain setup.

Epidemiological surveillance using social media signals has been proposed as a real-time complement to traditional disease reporting systems, which suffer from reporting lags of days to weeks. Brownstein et al. (2009) demonstrate that a news aggregation system monitoring online reports of disease outbreaks detected the H1N1 influenza pandemic several days ahead of official WHO notifications, establishing proof of concept for media-based surveillance. Subsequent work has extended this to user-generated content on social platforms, though the signal-to-noise ratio problem — distinguishing genuine disease reports from discussion, humor, and misinformation — remains a central challenge. Our detection pipeline draws on the alert threshold logic from Brownstein et al.'s monitoring system, adapting it to social media by incorporating a multi-class classifier that filters posts by report type before applying the anomaly detection component, which was designed for the higher-quality news text environment of their original system.
